title: ABA Model Rule 5.1: Responsibilities of Partners, Managers, and Supervisory Lawyers, with Official Comments
pub: ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct
author: American Bar Association

dom.t: AI supervision: Retained responsibility is not strict liability

st.t: AI supervision: Retained responsibility is not strict liability
st.an: Rule 5.1 directly supports the cluster’s distinction between affirmative, context-sensitive supervisory duties and automatic disciplinary liability. It requires reasonable compliance systems and supervision, while derivative responsibility arises only under specified conditions such as direction, knowing ratification, or knowing failure to take remedial action.
qs: [7] Apart from this Rule and Rule 8.4(a), a lawyer does not have disciplinary liability for the conduct of a partner, associate or subordinate.

mo.t: Cross-border outsourcing: Oversight follows the provider chain

kp.k: Managers must establish firm-wide professional compliance measures
kp.d: Rule 5.1(a) requires partners and lawyers with comparable managerial authority to make reasonable efforts to ensure that firm measures provide reasonable assurance of lawyers' compliance with professional conduct rules. This is a professional governance requirement, not an AI-specific rule or evidence of technological change.
qs: shall make reasonable efforts
measures giving reasonable assurance

kp.k: Managerial duties extend beyond traditional law firm partners
kp.d: Comment [1] includes professional corporation shareholders, members of other authorized practice associations, intermediate firm managers, and lawyers with comparable managerial authority in legal services organizations and enterprise or government law departments. The responsibility therefore encompasses managerial lawyers in both firms and organizational legal departments.
qs: lawyers who have intermediate managerial responsibilities in a firm
a law department of an enterprise or government agency

kp.k: Compliance systems must address operational risks and inexperienced lawyers
kp.d: Comment [2] identifies internal policies and procedures for detecting and resolving conflicts, identifying deadlines in pending matters, accounting for client funds and property, and ensuring proper supervision of inexperienced lawyers.
qs: detect and resolve conflicts of interest
ensure that inexperienced lawyers are properly supervised

kp.k: Required safeguards depend on firm structure and practice
kp.d: Comment [3] states that informal supervision and periodic compliance review ordinarily suffice in small firms of experienced lawyers, whereas large firms or practices presenting frequent difficult ethical problems may require more elaborate measures. It identifies confidential referral of junior lawyers' ethical concerns and continuing ethics education as possible measures, and warns partners against assuming universal compliance.
qs: can depend on the firm's structure and the nature of its practice
the ethical atmosphere of a firm can influence the conduct of all its members

kp.k: Direct supervisors have an independent reasonable-efforts duty
kp.d: Rule 5.1(b) requires lawyers with direct supervisory authority to make reasonable efforts to ensure subordinate lawyers' compliance. Comment [6] explains that a subordinate's misconduct could reveal deficient supervision even without the direction, ratification, or knowledge necessary for responsibility under paragraph (c).
qs: A lawyer having direct supervisory authority over another lawyer
there was no direction, ratification or knowledge of the violation

kp.k: Ordering or knowingly ratifying misconduct creates personal responsibility
kp.d: Rule 5.1(c)(1) makes a lawyer responsible for another lawyer's professional conduct violation when the lawyer orders the conduct or ratifies it with knowledge of the specific conduct. Comment [4] describes paragraph (c) as a principle of personal responsibility for another's acts.
qs: with knowledge of the specific conduct, ratifies the conduct involved
a general principle of personal responsibility for acts of another

kp.k: Known misconduct requires timely reasonable remedial action
kp.d: Rule 5.1(c)(2) imposes responsibility on qualifying managers or direct supervisors who know of misconduct while its consequences can still be avoided or mitigated but fail to take reasonable remedial action. Comment [5] makes the appropriate response depend on involvement and seriousness; its negotiation example requires a supervisor who knows of a subordinate's misrepresentation to correct the resulting misapprehension.
qs: knows of the conduct at a time when its consequences can be avoided or mitigated
fails to take reasonable remedial action

kp.k: Supervisory authority depends on factual responsibility for work
kp.d: Comment [5] treats supervisory authority as a factual question. Partners and comparable managers have at least indirect responsibility for all firm work; a partner or manager responsible for a particular matter ordinarily also supervises other firm lawyers working on it.
qs: Whether a lawyer has supervisory authority in particular circumstances is a question of fact.
at least indirect responsibility for all work being done by the firm

kp.k: Disciplinary responsibility differs from civil and criminal liability
kp.d: Comment [7] states that, apart from Rule 5.1 and Rule 8.4(a), lawyers do not have disciplinary liability for a partner's, associate's, or subordinate's conduct. Civil or criminal liability for another lawyer's conduct is a separate legal question outside these Rules' scope.
qs: Apart from this Rule and Rule 8.4(a)
a question of law beyond the scope of these Rules

kp.k: Supervision does not displace each lawyer's personal ethical duty
kp.d: Comment [8] preserves each firm's lawyer's personal duty to comply with professional conduct rules notwithstanding the additional duties imposed on managing and supervising lawyers, and cross-references Rule 5.2(a).
qs: do not alter the personal duty of each lawyer in a firm

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source makes no AI-related claims or predictions.
pts.d: ABA Model Rule 5.1 and its official comments prescribe managerial and supervisory responsibilities for lawyers. They do not discuss AI or claim that AI changes legal services, professional responsibilities, staffing, or legal markets. Applying these provisions to AI use would require an inference not made in the source.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: No evidence basis for an AI-related claim is offered.
pts.d: The document consists of an ABA Model Rule and explanatory comments, rather than empirical findings or predictions about AI. Its normative authority should not be treated as evidence of AI-driven change or as proof of adoption by any particular jurisdiction.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: No AI-related timeframe or conditions are stated.
pts.d: The supplied document is labeled 2026, but that label is not a forecast horizon. Conditions concerning managerial authority, supervision, knowledge of misconduct, and reasonable remedial action qualify the rule's general duties, not claims about AI.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: No group is identified as affected by AI.
pts.d: The rule addresses partners, lawyers with comparable managerial authority, supervisory lawyers, and other lawyers, including those in legal services organizations and enterprise or government law departments. It assigns general professional responsibilities without describing AI-specific effects on these groups.
